description: Law student and future aerospace engineer from Quetta, Pakistan. I build AI products (LexAI, an AI agent for phone checks) and love space, Earth data and AI ethics. I bring research, product vision, pitching and space-law insight. Looking for developers (Python/web), data/ML people familiar with NASA satellite data, and a designer. Let’s solve a real problem with NASA data
summary:
On a mission to Mars, Earth is minutes away by radio and there is no doctor on board for every question. AstroVital is an offline health self-monitoring tool that helps astronauts gather their health signals, understand what is normal for them, and know what to do next.

A two-minute daily check-in records vital signs, radiation dose, sleep, exercise, nutrition, mood and symptoms. A rules engine of 48 rules compares each reading with the astronaut's own baseline and shows a green, amber or red status. It is grouped by NASA's five spaceflight hazards and by eight body regions: bones, heart, brain and eyes (SANS), immune system, sleep and behavior, muscles, nutrition, and overall readiness. A 7-day trend alert catches slow decline early.

Every alert has a "Why?" panel showing the value, the threshold, the source, and whether the number is published or a design choice. Published anchors include NASA-STD-3001 radiation limits and RAD dose rates from Curiosity. A storm-shelter warning activates during solar particle events, and a crew view supports the medical office
details:
AstroVital has eight views: Overview, Health status, Daily check-in, Body regions, Trends, Crew view for the medical officer, Evidence, and Settings. The check-in can sync simulated smart-shirt, sweat-patch and dosimeter readings, then the astronaut adds how they feel.

How it works. Each of the 48 rules is a data object holding its thresholds, actions and evidence source. Signals are compared with the astronaut's personal baseline, the median of their first seven valid days. Sensor-quality gates mark worn-out or unreliable wearable readings instead of raising false alarms. Feeling fine does not clear a vision, motion-sickness or chest-pain alert without an objective check, and the app never claims to detect a cardiac event.

Decision support. The automation level can be set to Inform, Recommend or Guide, where each completed step is logged. A decision log and a report queue let ground teams review what the crew saw at the next communication window. A mission-context setting tightens overall alert sensitivity for deep-space transit.

Built with. It is built with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no libraries, and 39 automated tests check the rules.

Honesty. An evidence table maps every rule to NASA's Human Research Program risks and labels which thresholds are placeholders for flight surgeons to set.
